title: “Zlibrary my beloved”: Anthropic staff chats extolling piracy cited in Sony suit
gist: Music publishers including Sony, EMI and Warner Chappell sued Anthropic, arguing that the $1.5 billion book-authors settlement is too small to deter a company at a $2 trillion valuation and alleging its torrenting of LibGen and Pirate Library Mirror swept in thousands of copyrighted musical compositions. The complaint attacks the fair-use defense on market-harm grounds specific to lyrics and seeks an injunction plus a full accounting of Anthropic's training data, methods and model capabilities.

insights.claim: Music publishers argue that Anthropic's $1.5 billion settlement with authors, paid after admitting to pirating more than 7 million books to train AI, is not large enough to deter infringing conduct by a company with a $2 trillion valuation.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Plaintiffs are explicitly benchmarking damages to enterprise value rather than to actual harm — a framing that would sharply raise the expected cost of copyright exposure across frontier AI labs.
insights.quote: $1.5 billion is obviously not a large enough settlement to deter infringing conduct by a company that has parlayed such mass infringement into a staggering $2-trillion-dollar valuation
insights.locator: Some of the world’s leading music publishers

insights.claim: Publishers seek an injunction ending the AI training rather than damages alone, arguing that without one Anthropic will continue violating music copyrights while substituting for artists in their own markets.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Injunctive relief, not cash, is the tail risk for AI labs: an order restricting training data or model deployment is not something a balance sheet can absorb.
insights.locator: Pirated books that Anthropic allegedly plans to keep

insights.claim: Publishers demand that Anthropic be ordered to provide an accounting of its training data, training methods and known model capabilities so artists across media could assess how their works were acquired, ingested and how much they influenced a commercial model.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Forced training-data disclosure would be the single most consequential outcome of AI copyright litigation, converting a closely guarded trade secret into a discoverable record for every future plaintiff.
insights.locator: Anthropic closely guards its training data sources

insights.claim: The complaint alleges Anthropic's mass torrenting began in July 2021 when co-founder Benjamin Mann personally used BitTorrent to download and upload millions of pirated books from Library Genesis, with CEO Dario Amodei allegedly approving it; both are named individually as defendants.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Naming founders individually raises personal liability stakes and is a tactic likely to recur in AI copyright suits against other labs.

insights.claim: After the FBI shut down LibGen at the end of 2021 and Z-Library was also shut down quickly, Anthropic obtained a copy through the Pirate Library Mirror, with Mann allegedly directing employees to torrent it and messaging that the mirror dropped "just in time!"
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A documented pattern of routing around enforcement actions is exactly the willfulness evidence that drives statutory damages multipliers.
insights.locator: By the end of 2021, though, the FBI had shut down LibGen

insights.claim: Publishers say crawling the non-confidential catalogs of LibGen and PiLiMi showed bibliographic metadata indicating Anthropic torrented at least hundreds of books containing sheet music and song lyrics to compositions they own, with the full extent to be revealed in discovery.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The current evidentiary base is metadata inference; discovery is the catalyst that determines whether this scales into a much larger claim.
insights.locator: In total, they alleged that crawling through LibGen

insights.claim: Amodei testified in the book authors' litigation that Anthropic could have legally purchased copyrighted works but torrented them instead to avoid a "legal/practice/business slog," which the court summarized as downloading pirated books to avoid the trouble of paying for them.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Sworn testimony of a deliberate cost-avoidance choice, rather than inadvertence, is the strongest single fact against a good-faith defense.
insights.locator: Amodei testified during the book authors’ litigation

insights.claim: Publishers concede Anthropic denies using the torrented books to train commercial Claude models but argue the denial depends on how "training" is defined, alleging that a commercial Claude model was trained on synthetic data created by a non-commercial model that had itself trained on LibGen or PiLiMi text, and received reinforced feedback from such a model.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A transitive-contamination theory through synthetic data and RL feedback would make pipeline provenance, not just direct training corpora, legally relevant for every AI developer.
insights.quote: Anthropic has trained at least one of its commercially released Claude models using synthetic data created by a non-commercial AI model that was trained on text derived from LibGen and/or PiLiMi.
insights.locator: Publishers suspect Claude trained on hit songs

insights.claim: Recently unsealed documents show an Anthropic witness testified the company stopped training LLMs on LibGen but continued using the LibGen dataset in connection with its guardrails, checking whether long strings of output text too closely matched source text.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Retaining a pirated corpus for safety evaluation is a distinct legal exposure from training use and may not be covered by any transformative-use defense.

insights.claim: Anthropic's public response is that this is the third lawsuit from the same lawyers recycling allegations from cases already before the courts, and that training generative AI models is transformative fair use as the court held in Bartz.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Anthropic is betting the Bartz fair-use holding generalizes; if it does not extend to music, its litigation reserve assumptions need rerating.
insights.quote: Training generative AI models is a transformative fair use—as the court held in Bartz—and we will defend ourselves robustly.
insights.locator: A spokesperson for Anthropic provided Ars

insights.claim: The author notes the earlier fair use ruling hinged on book authors' inability to prove market harms or AI substitution in their markets, and publishers believe music rightsholders have a better chance of proving market harm than authors did.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Market harm is the fulcrum of AI copyright outcomes; the music case is the cleanest test of whether demonstrable substitution flips the fair-use analysis.

insights.claim: Publishers allege Anthropic publicly tracks the threat its AI products pose to song lyricists and knows that AI-generated songs currently topping music charts compete directly with the musicians whose songs allegedly trained the AI.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: If AI songs are demonstrably charting, the substitution evidence that was missing in the book case becomes available — the key fact to verify.
insights.locator: They’ve alleged that Anthropic publicly tracks the threat

insights.claim: The complaint cites the US Copyright Office's observation that outputs which are not substantially similar to a specific copyrighted work may still dilute royalty pools when they compete in the market for that type of work, including song lyrics.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Market dilution as a theory of harm decouples liability from output similarity, a doctrinal shift that would broadly expand AI copyright exposure.
insights.locator: Most glaringly, the US Copyright Office has

insights.claim: Publishers allege Claude fetches lyrics without copyright management information, generates lyrics even when users do not request them — for example returning copyrighted lyrics alongside a requested chord progression — and mashes actual lyrics with AI-generated ones when making "new" songs.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Unprompted verbatim reproduction is the behavior most likely to defeat a transformative-use argument, and is directly testable by the court.
insights.locator: According to publishers, Claude models will fetch lyrics

insights.claim: Publishers allege Anthropic workers repeatedly prompted models for copyrighted lyrics and encouraged output containing them while testing whether models could recommend comparable songs, and that Anthropic destroyed physical books to create unauthorized digital copies of hundreds of songbooks and sheet music collections.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Even the legally cleaner scan-and-destroy route for physical books is being challenged when the underlying works are compositions, narrowing the safe path to lawful data acquisition.
insights.locator: Anthropic seemingly designed the model to perform this way.

insights.claim: Music publishers emphasize that Anthropic never approached them to strike licensing deals as its biggest AI rivals have, and has never sought or obtained any license to exploit their copyrighted works for training or output.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Competitors' licensing deals become the benchmark for what Anthropic should have paid — a ready-made damages anchor and a competitive argument for labs that licensed early.
